one_line: NASA lit a 94-cm-long sheet of cotton-fibreglass fabric inside an empty cargo spacecraft after it left the ISS, the first large fire deliberately set in orbit, to see whether a fire in microgravity keeps growing or settles to a steady size.
summary: Saffire-I burned a 40.6 cm x 94 cm sheet of SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric inside the uncrewed Cygnus OA-6 cargo module on 14 June 2016, after it left the ISS. This was about ten times larger in each dimension than any earlier microgravity flame-spread sample. Cabin air (about 21.7% O2, near 1 atm) was drawn through a flow duct at about 20 cm/s, and the sample was ignited at its upstream edge. The concurrent flame settled to a steady length of about 40 mm and spread steadily at 1.8 mm/s over about 84 cm for 420 s, releasing about 1.2 kW. On Earth, upward spread over this fabric accelerates. A contingency opposed-flow burn over the last ~10 cm spread at 1.3 mm/s; this fabric cannot burn downward in 1 g. Spread was slower than in the small BASS duct at half the flow, which the investigators attribute to duct size. The fire used about 0.2 percentage points of O2 and raised cabin pressure about 0.3 kPa. A steady flame size lets designers bound a fire's heat release.

question.text: Saffire-I asked two questions. (1) How rapidly does a large fire grow in low gravity, and does flame spread over a large, realistic piece of fabric reach a steady spread rate and a limiting flame size, or keep accelerating as upward fires do on Earth? (2) How do low-g flammability limits compare with NASA's normal-gravity material screening test (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1)? Saffire-I addressed the first; Saffire-II (PSI-99) addressed the second. The motivation is that all earlier microgravity flame-spread tests used samples no larger than about 10 cm in length and width, in small chambers, while a real spacecraft fire would be much larger. Designers have therefore relied on terrestrial fire data and standards, which carry large uncertainty for missions far from Earth. Full-scale fire tests had never been possible in a crewed vehicle; an expendable cargo vehicle after it leaves the ISS removes the risk to crew.

physics.text: A flame spreading over a thin solid heats the fuel ahead of it until the fuel pyrolyses; the vapour mixes with oxygen and burns. On Earth, upward (concurrent) spread over a fabric is driven by a buoyant plume whose induced velocity grows with height, so the heated region, the flame and the spread rate all keep growing: upward fires accelerate. In orbit there is no buoyancy; the only flow is the imposed ventilation, here 20 cm/s, which is in the range of spacecraft cabin air circulation. In concurrent flow the flame and its hot plume extend downstream over unburnt fuel and preheat it, while the fuel behind the flame burns out. For a thin fuel, the burning (pyrolysis) zone has a length L_p set by how long the fuel takes to burn out, and the spread rate V_f is L_p divided by that burnout time. If the flame length is limited by the oxygen supply carried by a fixed forced flow, the flame, the pyrolysis zone and the spread rate can all reach steady values, so the fire stops growing. In opposed flow (the air moving against the spread, like downward burning on Earth), spread is governed by heat conducted forward from the flame's leading edge and is usually slower. A thin fabric that cannot spread downward on Earth because the strong buoyant flow blows it off can spread in a gentle forced opposed flow in microgravity. Two scale effects matter for comparisons with small experiments: a wider sample has less oxygen supply per unit width from the sides, and a small duct accelerates the flow around a flame because the hot gas expands, which increases spread rate.

sources.quote: In contrast, upward (concurrent) flame spread at normal gravity on Earth is usually found to be accelerating so that the flame size grows with time.
The forced airflow was 20–25 cm/s, which is typical of air circulation speeds in a spacecraft.
Compared to a wide sample, a narrow sample has more effective oxygen transport across the width of the sample.
This is attributed to the effect of flow acceleration in the smaller tunnels as a result of hot gas expansion.
An upward-spreading (concurrent-flow) flame on Earth is nearly always more hazardous than a downward-spreading (opposed-flow) flame.

equations.meaning: Steady concurrent spread over a thin fuel. $V_f$ spread rate of the pyrolysis front (mm/s); $L_p$ steady pyrolysis length, the burning zone between the burnout front and the pyrolysis front (mm); $t_b$ local burnout time of the fuel (s). A steady state needs $L_p$ to stop growing, which happens when the forced flow limits the flame length; in 1 g buoyant upward spread $L_p$ keeps growing and the flame accelerates. Li et al. use this definition of burnout time to compare the 5 cm and 41 cm Saffire samples.

sources.quote: While steady state pyrolysis lengths were similar, the 5 cm wide sample had a slightly larger spread rate (by ∼13%) and a shorter burnout time (pyrolysis length over spread rate) compared to the 41 cm wide sample.

equations.meaning: Heat release rate of a steadily spreading flame over a sheet. $\dot Q$ (W); $m''_c$ areal density of the combustible part (kg/m2; SIBAL: 0.75 x 18 mg/cm2 = 0.135 kg/m2); $W$ sample width (m); $V_f$ spread rate (m/s); $\Delta h_c$ heat of combustion (J/kg, about 16 MJ/kg for cellulose, textbook value); $\eta$ fraction of the cotton actually burned (combustion efficiency). For Saffire-I ($W$ = 0.406 m, $V_f$ = 1.8 mm/s) complete combustion gives about 1.6 kW, of the same order as the investigators' estimate of 1200 +/- 300 W; smoulder residue and incomplete burnout lower $\eta$. Valid only once the spread is steady.

sources.quote: Average flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s; estimated average flame power is 1200 +/- 300 W

equations.meaning: Complete combustion of cellulose consumes one O2 molecule per CO2 produced, so the drop in cabin O2 mole fraction equals the rise in CO2 mole fraction ($x$, mole fraction or %). This is how the investigators derived the O2 decrement from the CO2 sensor (21.7 to 21.5%), and it matches the +0.21 percentage-point CO2 rise in the PSI sensor file. It neglects CO, soot and absorption by the vehicle's CO2 removal (if any) during the burn.

sources.quote: i Derived from measured CO2 production and referenced to initial O2 concentration reported by ISS.

equations.meaning: Thermal-regime (de Ris) opposed-flow spread rate over a thermally thin solid. $\lambda_g$ gas conductivity (W/m K); $T_f$, $T_v$, $T_\infty$ flame, pyrolysis and ambient temperatures (K); $\rho_s c_s \tau$ solid heat capacity per unit area (J/m2 K), here with $\tau$ the half-thickness. Textbooks differ on this convention: de Ris's original form uses $\sqrt{2}$ with the half-thickness, and some texts pair $\pi/4$ with the full thickness, so the coefficient depends on that choice. It predicts a spread rate independent of the opposed flow when chemistry is fast and radiation negligible. It is the reference against which the Saffire-I opposed rate (1.3 mm/s at 20 cm/s) and the BASS opposed rates can be compared.

apparatus.text: The Saffire flight unit (about 53 x 90 x 133 cm) was a flow duct with an adjoining avionics bay, separated by a Lexan panel. It was strapped into the Cygnus Pressurized Cargo Module (PCM) and was open to the cabin air at both ends. Fans at the top (outlet) of the duct drew air through a flow straightener at the bottom; the duct cross-section was about 18 x 20 in (about 46 x 51 cm; a later paper gives a 25 cm duct height on each side of the sample and a 45 cm width). Two anemometers, one on each side of the sample, measured the air speed and fed the fan control loop. The single sample card sat in the middle of the duct. Hot-wire igniters were woven into the fabric along the upstream edge (main igniter) and the downstream edge (redundant igniter). Two cameras in the avionics bay viewed one face of the whole sample; a green LED was switched on 1 s in every 3 s to show the pyrolysis front. Four radiometers (two viewing the front and two the back, each pair upstream and downstream) measured broadband radiation. Six thermocouples were sewn into the fabric at the centreline, with beads at several heights above the surface, at two streamwise stations; six more measured plume temperature, and one the inlet temperature. Solid-state sensors measured O2 (at the avionics bay inlet), CO2, pressure and humidity. A smoke wire at the sample leading edge gave flow visualisation before and after the burns. Sensor data were logged at about 30 Hz (0.033 s steps) and cameras recorded at about 30 frames/s.

procedure.text: Saffire-I launched in the Cygnus OA-6 PCM on 22 March 2016 and stayed unpowered while the vehicle was berthed to the ISS. Before unberthing, the crew checked that the duct inlet and outlet were not blocked by stowed trash. After Cygnus left the ISS and moved to a separate orbit, the ground (Orbital ATK and NASA flight operations teams) powered the unit, ran a built-in test, recorded pre-test smoke-wire flow visualisation (F1), and sent the RUN command. On 14 June 2016 the fan set the flow to about 20 cm/s and, about 60 s into the recording, the upstream igniter was powered for 8 s (about 182 W measured; the 2017 slides give 165 W, 4.1 W/cm of width). The flame then spread downstream (concurrent flow) until the 420 s allotted burn time ended and the fan was switched off, which extinguished the flame at once. About 90% of the fabric had burned, so the contingency opposed-flow test was run: about 11 minutes later the downstream igniter was powered for 8 s and the flame spread upstream into the flow over the remaining ~10 cm, for about 70 s. Post-test flow visualisation (F2) followed. Images were compressed on board and downlinked over the following days, limited to 20 Gbit in total; selected raw (uncompressed) frames were then requested. The relays were opened on 19 June 2016 and Cygnus re-entered on 21 June.

psi_data.summary: PSI-98 holds 76 files (12.25 GB). Almost all of it (61 zips, 12.18 GB, not downloaded) is imagery: for each run (S1, S2, F1, F2) and camera (C1, C2) there are on-board jpegs, distortion-corrected ('Mapped') jpegs, raw camera frames (DistroMaster, with the 8-byte offset fixed), demosaiced TIFFs, and PNGs annotated with exposure and gain, plus checkerboard distortion grids. The S1 sets are split into parts and are the largest (the annotated PNG sets alone are 1.0-1.5 GB per part). What is usable now are the downloaded sensor workbooks. 'Sample 1/2 Sensor Data Complete TM graphs.xlsx' (25 MB each) hold a 'Calibrated Data' sheet at about 30 Hz for 660 s per run: fan speed, CO2, O2, two anemometers, ambient pressure, four radiometers (raw and baseline-subtracted, labelled upstream/downstream, front/back), humidity, inlet temperature, six plume and six sample thermocouples, radiometer temperatures, igniter current and voltage, avionics housekeeping and control flags; plus a 'Camera Data' sheet of per-frame exposure and gain. 'Telemetry Data Good Process Version.xlsx' holds the low-rate real-time telemetry (radiometers, anemometers, fan tachometer, igniters for all 9 Saffire-II-style channels) and Cygnus vehicle data (PCM air temperature and pressure, smoke detectors, cabin fan pressure rise, body rates, accelerations). Two docx files hold the sensor plots. The MergeResult xlsx lists every image file by timestamp, whether it was received or corrupted, and its zip (about 36,000 images each for S1 and S2). No reduced data (flame position vs time, spread rates) are in PSI; the published results come from NASA technical reports and journal papers.

findings.claim: In concurrent flow at about 20 cm/s and 21.7% O2 (falling to 21.5%) near 1 atm, the flame over the 40.6 cm x 94 cm SIBAL sheet reached a steady state: it spread at a constant average 1.8 mm/s, and the flame length reached a plateau of about 40 mm. It burned about 84 cm of the 94 cm sheet during the 420 s allotted. On Earth the same configuration (upward burning) consumes the whole sample with an accelerating flame. This answers the main Saffire question: a large concurrent fire in microgravity, under forced ventilation, need not keep growing.

sources.quote: For the concurrent flame, the length reaches a plateau value of around 40 mm, while the opposed-flow flame is a bit shorter at 24 mm.
1-1 182 W 8 s 420 s ~ 84 cm 1.8 mm/s Complete Acceleratory
The downloaded test data show that a concurrent (downstream) spreading flame over thin fabrics in microgravity reaches a steady spread rate and a limiting length.

findings.claim: The opposed-flow flame (spreading into the 20 cm/s flow, ~21.5% O2) burned the remaining ~10 cm of fabric in about 70 s at an average 1.3 mm/s, with a flame length of about 24 mm. In 1 g this fabric does not spread downward (burn length ~0). So for this material, opposed-flow spread is possible in microgravity at a cabin-like ventilation speed but not on Earth. The concurrent flame spread about 1.4 times faster than the opposed flame.

sources.quote: The average concurrent-flow flame spread rate is 1.8 mm/s. The opposed-flow flame average spread rate 1.3 mm/s.

findings.claim: The average flame power of the concurrent fire was estimated at 1200 +/- 300 W. This is a 40.6-cm-wide flame front; the 5-cm-wide SIBAL samples of Saffire-II gave about 200 W.

findings.claim: The concurrent flame was unsteady at first: flame length and brightness oscillated at about 1.4 Hz until about 90 s into the test, then settled, with small fluctuations at about 0.75 Hz persisting for the whole burn. The cause is unknown; the investigators suggest a flow oscillation present even in cold flow, or flame interaction with the flow in the duct entrance.

sources.quote: Initially the flame length fluctuated at about 1.4 Hz before finally becoming more stable at about 90 s
However, subtle fluctuations in flame length and brightness persisted for the duration of the test albeit at a slightly slower frequency of around 0.75 Hz.

findings.claim: Flame appearance: at ignition the flame was bright yellow and vigorous; it soon developed a blue base with orange radiation from incandescent soot. Behind the flame, exothermic smoulder spots kept burning leftover fuel. When the air flow was switched off at the end of the allotted time, the flame went out immediately.

sources.quote: At ignition, the flame was mostly bright yellow and relatively vigorous but it soon developed a blue base and a pattern of orange radiation coming from incandescent soot
The flame burned the entire allotted test time of about 7 min. at which point the air flow was shut off and the flame immediately extinguished

findings.claim: Scale and duct size matter. The Saffire-I concurrent flame (1.8 mm/s at 20 cm/s in a ~46 x 51 cm duct) spread more slowly than BASS flames over the same fabric in the 7.6 cm SPICE duct, even though the Saffire sample was much wider and the flow was twice as fast. BASS 2-cm strips spread at 2.55 mm/s at about 10 cm/s, and BASS's linear concurrent fits (printed as V_F = -0.20 U + 0.56 and -0.15 U + 0.07 mm/s on an axis where concurrent flow is negative; written with U as the concurrent speed in cm/s, V_F = 0.20U + 0.56 or 0.15U + 0.07) extrapolate to about 3.1-4.6 mm/s at 20 cm/s (our extrapolation). The investigators attribute this to flow acceleration from hot-gas expansion in the smaller tunnels, and conclude that concurrent spread is more sensitive to duct dimensions than anticipated. Small-duct microgravity data can therefore overestimate concurrent spread in an open cabin.

sources.quote: Compared to previous microgravity work in smaller tunnels, the flame in the larger tunnel spread more slowly, even for a wider sample. This is attributed to the effect of flow acceleration in the smaller tunnels as a result of hot gas expansion.
Concurrent flame spread (with the wind) was shown to be more sensitive to the flow duct dimension than previously anticipated.

findings.claim: Sample width effect: a 5-cm-wide SIBAL strip burned on Saffire-II at the same 20 cm/s spread at 2.1 mm/s versus 1.8 mm/s for the 40.6-cm sheet (the model paper says about 13% faster; 2.1/1.8 is 17%), with a similar steady pyrolysis length and shorter burnout time. Part of the difference is the higher starting O2 (22.1% vs 21.7%). A 3-D transient model attributes the narrow sample's shorter burnout time to more effective oxygen transport across its width; neither source splits the spread-rate difference between this and the O2 difference. The large sample also showed an initial overshoot of pyrolysis length before reaching steady state, which the model explains by flow reduction in the growing boundary layer.

sources.quote: The flame spread rate for the 5-cm-wide sample is marginally faster compared to the spread rate for the 40.6-cm-wide sample for the same flow speed of 20 cm/s (2.1 compared to 1.8 mm/s).

While steady state pyrolysis lengths were similar, the 5 cm wide sample had a slightly larger spread rate (by ∼13%) and a shorter burnout time (pyrolysis length over spread rate) compared to the 41 cm wide sample.
Compared to a wide sample, a narrow sample has more effective oxygen transport across the width of the sample.
However, the pyrolysis length exhibited an initial overshoot before reaching steady state for the large sample.
The modeling results reveal that flow reduction in a growing boundary layer along the sample surface accounts for the overshoot of the flame length observed for the large sample.

findings.claim: Effect on the vehicle (our analysis of the PSI sensor files). During the concurrent burn, CO2 at the Saffire sensor rose from 0.426% to 0.632% (+0.21 percentage points), consistent with the investigators' O2 drop of 21.7% to 21.5% derived from CO2. The Saffire ambient pressure rose from 14.843 to about 14.888 psia (+0.045 psi, +0.31 kPa, +0.3%), peaking near the end of the burn and decaying after the fan stopped. The Cygnus PCM pressure rose from 14.488 to 14.537 psi (+0.34 kPa) and the PCM air temperature from 19.98 to 20.18 C. The opposed burn added only +0.02 percentage points CO2. The investigators describe the oxygen use as '1.5 of the available oxygen' (unit missing in the source).

findings.claim: Radiometer records (our analysis) bracket the concurrent burn. Baseline-subtracted radiation at the upstream pair rose from ignition (t = 60 s) to 139 mW/cm2 at t = 225 s. The downstream pair peaked at 145-149 mW/cm2 at t = 343 s as the flame passed them. Signal above 5 mW/cm2 lasted from t = 65 s to t = 485 s, i.e. about 420 s, matching the reported burn time and ending when the fan stopped (anemometers fall to ~0.1 cm/s by t = 500 s). For the opposed burn, only the downstream radiometers responded (peak 18-21 mW/cm2 at t = 105 s). The signal fell to baseline by t = 138 s, about 75 s after ignition, while the fan was still running, consistent with burnout of the remaining fuel. The radiometers' view geometry is not documented in PSI, so these are relative signals, not flame emissive power.

findings.claim: The fan control loop held the measured air speed near 20 cm/s by cutting fan speed from about 6340 to about 5100 RPM as the flame grew (t = 60-200 s), then raising it again. During the burn the two anemometers diverged (one rising to ~21.6 cm/s, the other falling to ~18.4 cm/s), so the fire itself perturbed the duct flow. The free-stream velocity over the flame is therefore known only to about +/-1-2 cm/s.

relevance.text: Saffire-I is the first measurement of how a realistically large fabric fire behaves in a spacecraft. Its key result is that, with forced ventilation of about 20 cm/s and no buoyancy, a concurrent flame over a thin charring fabric does not keep growing as it would on Earth. It reaches a steady spread rate (1.8 mm/s) and a limiting size (flame length ~40 mm, about 1.2 kW for a 40 cm front). The investigators note that a bounded flame size lets designers set the heat release rate a fire can impose on the vehicle. The opposed-flow burn confirms that a fabric which cannot burn downward in 1 g can burn against a cabin-like flow in orbit, so the 1-g downward configuration is not conservative. The duct-size effect means small-chamber microgravity flammability data (BASS, glovebox tests) are not directly transferable to an open cabin: here the larger enclosure gave slower spread. Vehicle impact was small: about 0.2 percentage points of O2 consumed and a 0.3 kPa pressure rise in the Cygnus PCM. This bounds the effect of one ~1 kW, 7-minute fire in a cargo-module-sized volume, not a worst case. The vehicle telemetry (smoke detectors, pressure, temperature) gives a first data set for detection and habitability modelling. The result applies to one thin cellulosic fabric at about 21% O2 and 1 atm; it is not a flammability limit and does not cover thick fuels or exploration atmospheres.

sources.quote: The existence of a flame size limit has important considerations for spacecraft fire safety as it can be used to establish the heat release rate in the vehicle.
Flame spread over a large thin charring surface in low-gravity showed that steady flame spread was possible (unlike normal gravity).

habitat_conditions.text: Saffire-I burned in Cygnus cabin air: 21.7% O2 at the start (ISS reading at hatch closure), falling to 21.5%, at about 14.5-14.8 psi (99.9-102.3 kPa depending on the sensor). This is essentially the Earth sea-level reference (20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa), and slightly O2-enriched. It is far from the exploration atmospheres in the shared reference: a Moon habitat at 30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less, and spacesuits at 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa. Higher O2 mole fraction generally raises spread rates and flame temperatures, so these results do not bound fire growth in such atmospheres. The Saffire team listed elevated-O2, reduced-pressure flame behaviour as a follow-on objective, to be compared with Saffire-I to III. The 20 cm/s flow is representative of cabin ventilation.

earth_benefits.text: Studying fire in a small, sealed vehicle is relevant to fire safety in other confined spaces such as mines, aircraft and submarines. The purely forced-flow data also give clean validation cases for flame-spread models (e.g. the CWRU 3-D transient model) used for both space and terrestrial fire scenarios.

limitations.text: Only one large sample. There was a single concurrent burn and a contingency opposed burn over only ~10 cm of leftover fabric, at a single flow speed and O2 level, so there is no repeatability and the opposed result rests on about 70 s of burning.

Data quality: the PSI record dates (start 2001-03-02, end 2008-02-28) do not match the experiment (launch 22 March 2016, burn 14 June 2016, relays opened 19 June 2016); the identity dates here use the external sources. The PSI 'proposalTitle' ('Characterization of Smoke from Microgravity Fires for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection') belongs to a smoke investigation, not Saffire.

Data quality: the experimental table gives thickness '0.37' in a cm column, but the published value is 0.37 mm; it also swaps length and width (length 40.6, width 94) relative to all documents (40.6 cm wide x 94 cm long). The table's ignition power (182 W) matches the raw igniter data, while the 2017 slides say 165 W.

Data quality: the Saffire O2 sensor reads ~22.6% before ignition, against the 21.7% ISS reading used by the investigators. Pressure differs between the Saffire sensor (14.84 psia) and the Cygnus PCM sensor (14.49 psi).
Data quality: the ICES 2016 slide (NTRS 20170002628) says OA-6 unberthed on 'June 22', which conflicts with the 14 June operations date in the same slide and the sensor timestamps.
The external ICES 2017 abstract says the fire 'consumed 1.5 of the available oxygen' with no unit; the table in the same deck gives 21.7 to 21.5% O2. The exact meaning is unclear.
Saffire-I sensor-derived values in findings (pressure, CO2, radiometer and thermocouple peaks, fan speed) are our computations from the PSI workbooks, not published numbers.
No text addressed to an AI or unrelated instructions were found in the PSI-98 documents.
